question: How do I get my criminal record sealed or expunged, how long do I have to wait, and what does it cost?

groups: records and files relating to the arrest
elapsed from the date of arrest

gold_sections.why: A person tried and acquitted by the trial court is entitled to expunction of the arrest records (subject to the criminal-episode exception).
Expunction after conviction followed by a pardon or other relief on the basis of actual innocence.
Expunction after conviction followed by a pardon for another reason.
Who can use the no-conviction grounds: released, charge did not end in a final conviction and is no longer pending, and no court-ordered community supervision except for a Class C misdemeanor.
No charge presented: waiting periods of 180 days (Class C), one year (Class B or A) or three years (felony) from arrest, or sooner if the prosecutor certifies the records are not needed.
A filed charge dismissed or quashed because of a veterans, mental health or pretrial intervention program, absence of probable cause, or a void charge.
Expunction once prosecution is barred because the limitations period has expired.
No expunction of an acquittal when the person was convicted of, or remains subject to prosecution for, another offense in the same criminal episode.
A person who absconded after release on bail cannot use the waiting-period or limitations grounds.
After an acquittal the trial court must advise of the right to expunction and enter the order within 30 days on request.
Where to file: an ex parte petition in a district court for the county of arrest or of the alleged offense.
Fine-only offenses: the petition may be filed in a justice court or a municipal court of record.
The petition must be verified and list the person's identifying data, the arrest and every agency and entity holding records.
Hearing set no earlier than the 30th day after filing; notice to each listed entity; $25 for each entity that cannot receive electronic notice.
The court decides and shall order expunction when the person is entitled.
The petitioner or a protesting agency may appeal as in other civil cases.
When the order is final the clerk sends it to DPS, the Office of Court Administration and each listed entity; $25 per entity that cannot take electronic delivery.
Listed agencies return or obliterate the records and delete index references.
Effect of a final expunction order: the records may not be used and the person may deny the arrest.

Expunction fees: district court civil ex parte filing fee, $100 in a justice or municipal court of record, waivers for prompt acquittal petitions and veterans or mental health court graduates, possible refund.
The state consolidated civil fee ($137) that district clerks collect on filing any civil case, one component of the civil filing fee.
Discharge and dismissal from deferred adjudication; the judge must grant or explain nondisclosure eligibility and the earliest date.
Deferred adjudication for a first, nonviolent misdemeanor: the court issues the nondisclosure order without a petition (at discharge or on the 180th day) after a $28 fee.
Other deferred adjudication: petition after discharge for most misdemeanors, after two years for listed misdemeanors, after five years for felonies; best interest of justice.
Deferred adjudication for first DWI or BWI: petition two years after discharge, barred if the offense caused a collision with another person.
Community supervision after a misdemeanor conviction: petition on completion or two years later for listed misdemeanors.
Community supervision after a first DWI conviction: two years (ignition interlock) or five years after completion.
Misdemeanor convictions: petition on completion of the sentence if fine-only, otherwise two years after; violent or sexual offenses barred.
First DWI conviction: three years (ignition interlock) or five years after completing the sentence.
Conditions for every nondisclosure order: no new non-traffic offense during supervision and the waiting period; offenses that always bar nondisclosure.
Petition filed in person, electronically or by mail with the civil case filing fee; notice to the state; hearing unless the state is silent for 45 days and the court finds entitlement.
After the order: clerk to DPS within 15 business days, DPS seals within 10 business days and forwards, agencies seal within 30 business days.
Effect of nondisclosure: no need to disclose the proceeding on employment, information or licensing applications.
Nondisclosed information is excepted from public information requests and the person may deny the proceeding.

nuggets.text: A person who was tried and acquitted by the trial court is entitled to have all records and files of the arrest expunged (subject to the same-criminal-episode exception).
nuggets.quote: acquitted by the trial court, except as provided by Article 55A.151

nuggets.text: Expunction without an acquittal or pardon requires that the charge did not end in a final conviction, is no longer pending, and that there was no court-ordered community supervision (including deferred adjudication) except for a Class C misdemeanor.
nuggets.quote: the charge, if any, has not resulted in a final conviction and is no longer pending; and (3) there was no court-ordered community supervision under Chapter 42A for the offense, other than for a Class C misdemeanor

nuggets.text: If no charge was ever presented, a Class C misdemeanor arrest can be expunged once at least 180 days have passed since the arrest.
nuggets.quote: at least 180 days have elapsed from the date of arrest if the arrest for which the expunction was sought was for an offense punishable as a Class C misdemeanor

nuggets.text: If no charge was ever presented, a Class B or A misdemeanor arrest can be expunged once at least one year has passed since the arrest.
nuggets.quote: at least one year has elapsed from the date of arrest if the arrest for which the expunction was sought was for an offense punishable as a Class B or A misdemeanor

nuggets.text: If no charge was ever presented, a felony arrest can be expunged once at least three years have passed since the arrest.
nuggets.quote: at least three years have elapsed from the date of arrest if the arrest for which the expunction was sought was for an offense punishable as a felony

nuggets.text: An arrest can also be expunged once prosecution is no longer possible because the statute of limitations has expired.
nuggets.quote: prosecution of the person for the offense for which the person was arrested is no longer possible because the limitations period has expired

nuggets.text: The person files an ex parte petition for expunction in a district court for the county where the person was arrested or where the offense allegedly occurred.
nuggets.quote: file an ex parte petition for expunction in a district court for the county in which: (1) the petitioner was arrested; or (2) the offense was alleged to have occurred

nuggets.text: In district court the petitioner pays the fee charged for filing an ex parte petition in a civil action (in addition to other fees required by law).
nuggets.quote: a petitioner seeking expunction of a criminal record in a district court shall pay the fee charged for filing an ex parte petition in a civil action in district court

nuggets.text: In a justice court or municipal court of record the expunction filing fee is $100.
nuggets.quote: a petitioner seeking expunction of a criminal record in a justice court or a municipal court of record under Chapter 55A shall pay a fee of $100 for filing an ex parte petition for expunction

nuggets.text: After deferred adjudication for a first-time misdemeanor that is not DWI, BWI or one of the listed assaultive, sexual, family, public-order, weapons or organized-crime offenses, the court that placed the person on deferred adjudication must issue an order of nondisclosure without a petition once the person is discharged and meets Section 411.074.
nuggets.quote: the court that placed the person on deferred adjudication community supervision shall issue an order of nondisclosure of criminal history record information under this subchapter

nuggets.text: For that automatic nondisclosure order the person must pay a $28 fee to the court clerk.
nuggets.quote: The person must pay a $28 fee to the clerk of the court before the court issues the order.

nuggets.text: After deferred adjudication for a felony, the person may petition for nondisclosure only on or after the fifth anniversary of the discharge and dismissal.
nuggets.quote: the fifth anniversary of the discharge and dismissal, if the offense for which the person was placed on deferred adjudication was a felony

nuggets.text: A first-time misdemeanor conviction that was not fine-only can be the subject of a nondisclosure petition two years after the sentence is completed (fine-only misdemeanors immediately on completion).
nuggets.quote: the second anniversary of the date of completion of the person's sentence, if the offense of which the person was convicted was a misdemeanor other than a misdemeanor described by Subdivision (1)

nuggets.text: Nondisclosure is never available if the offense, or any prior offense, requires sex-offender registration or is aggravated kidnapping, murder, capital murder, trafficking, injury to a child, elderly or disabled person, child abandonment, a protective-order violation, stalking, or another family-violence offense.
nuggets.quote: the person requests the order of nondisclosure for, or the person has been previously convicted of or placed on deferred adjudication community supervision for: (A) an offense requiring registration as a sex offender under Chapter 62, Code of Criminal Procedure

nuggets.text: A nondisclosure petition must be accompanied by the fee that generally applies to filing a civil case.
nuggets.quote: The petition must be accompanied by payment of a fee that generally applies to the filing of a civil case.

answer: Texas has two remedies, and a judge decides both [N7][N10]. Expunction erases arrest records [N1]. You qualify if you were acquitted at trial [N1], or if the charge did not end in a final conviction, is no longer pending, and you got no court-ordered probation or deferred adjudication except for a Class C misdemeanor [N2]. If no charge was ever filed, wait 180 days after the arrest for a Class C misdemeanor [N3], one year for a Class B or A misdemeanor [N4], or three years for a felony [N5]. A filed charge that was dismissed can be expunged once the statute of limitations runs out [N6]. File a sworn ex parte petition in the district court of the county where you were arrested or the offense allegedly happened [N7]; you pay the court's civil ex parte filing fee [N8], or $100 in a justice court or municipal court of record [N9]. Nondisclosure (Texas sealing) hides records from the public after deferred adjudication or some convictions [N10][N13]. For a first nonviolent misdemeanor on deferred adjudication, the court that supervised you issues the order without a petition [N10] once you pay a $28 fee [N11]. Otherwise you petition and pay the usual civil filing fee [N15]: five years after discharge for a felony deferred adjudication [N12], or two years after finishing the sentence for a first misdemeanor conviction that was not fine-only [N13]. Sex-offender-registration offenses, murder, family violence and other listed offenses, even past ones, bar sealing [N14].

gaps: The expunction path is drawn for the general ex parte petition (Articles 55A.251-55A.255). An acquitted person can instead ask the trial court for an order within 30 days of the acquittal (Article 55A.201), and a mistaken-identity applicant goes through the felony prosecutor and gets an order without a hearing (Article 55A.256); neither is drawn.
Article 55A.254(a) sets the hearing no earlier than the 30th day after filing. That is a minimum wait, not a deadline, so it is not drawn as a timer.

The nondisclosure path follows Section 411.0725 (deferred adjudication other than first nonviolent misdemeanors). Sections 411.073, 411.0726, 411.0731, 411.0735 and 411.0736 use the same petition, notice and best-interest steps with different waiting periods; Section 411.072 needs no petition (the court acts at discharge or on the 180th day after the person was placed on deferred adjudication, after a $28 fee).

Section 411.0745(e) lets the court skip the hearing only if the state does not ask for one before the 45th day and the court finds entitlement and best interest. The model routes the 45-day timer to the court's decision; whether a hearing is actually held then sits inside the decision.
The clerk, DPS and agency sealing deadlines in Section 411.075 state no consequence for missing them (consequence 'unstated').
After the order is sent (Article 55A.351), DPS must also notify federal depositories and private entities (Article 55A.352); not drawn.

version_flags: No section relied on carries an '(Effective ...)' or '(Effective until ...)' heading as of 2026-10-10.
CCP art. 55A.356(d) and (e) were repealed by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., ch. 850 (S.B. 1667), eff. September 1, 2025; the answer does not depend on them.
Chapter 55A recodified the former expunction chapter (Chapter 55, Articles 55.01-55.06); older guides cite the Article 55 numbers.
local_option: The dollar cost of a district court petition depends on the county's civil fee schedule. A Class C or other fine-only arrest can be filed in a justice court or a municipal court of record, but only cities that have a municipal court of record offer that venue.
notes: Texas has no general automatic sealing for adult records: expunction (CCP ch. 55A) destroys arrest records for people not finally convicted (or acquitted or pardoned); nondisclosure (Gov't Code ch. 411, subch. E-1) seals deferred adjudication and some misdemeanor and first-DWI records from the public, with the narrow exception of Section 411.072, where the court issues the order without a petition. Left out of the 15 nuggets: the prosecutor certification that lets a no-charge arrest skip the wait (55A.052(a)(4)); dismissals that qualify immediately (55A.053: veterans, mental health or pretrial intervention programs, absence of probable cause, void charge); absconding bars the waiting-period and limitations grounds (55A.154); fee waivers for acquittal petitions filed within 30 days (102.0061(c)) and for veterans or mental health court graduates (102.0061(d), 55A.203(c)); possible refund of the district court fee (102.0061(e)); $25 per listed entity that cannot receive electronic notice (55A.254(f), 55A.351(b-3)); the state consolidated civil fee of $137 (Local Gov't Code 133.151) as one part of the civil filing fee; 411.0725(e) misdemeanor timing (on discharge, or two years for Penal Code ch. 20, 21, 22, 25, 42, 43, 46); first DWI or BWI rules (411.0726: two years; 411.0731: two or five years; 411.0736: three or five years, depending on an ignition interlock); 411.0735(c-1) bars violent or sexual misdemeanors other than simple assault; effects (55A.401: deny the arrest; 411.0755 and Gov't Code 552.142: no need to disclose, may deny the proceeding). The felony five-year and misdemeanor two-year nondisclosure waits are stated as ordinals ('fifth anniversary', 'second anniversary'), which the slot checker cannot match to a number, so they appear as deadline nuggets (N12, N13) but not in slots.deadline. Juvenile sealing (Family Code ch. 58, subch. C-1) and the minor's fine-only expunction (CCP 45A.463) are separate regimes, not covered here.
